title: The Five-Step Method of True Qi Circulation
excerpt: The very core of life's activity — the circulation of true qi.

inline.s: The core of life's activity — the circulation of true qi.
The medicine for healing lies within yourself; what matters most is constancy and perseverance.

True qi is the material foundation and the motive source of the body's life activity, and the key to resisting illness, building immunity, and strengthening health and years. The Suwen, in the chapter “Separating and Uniting the True and the Evasive Qi,” says:
“True qi is the qi of the channels.”
Therefore, when true qi is abundant the body is healthy; when true qi is insufficient a hundred illnesses arise; and when true qi vanishes life comes to an end.

The Zhenqi Circulation Method (called for short the “True Method”) has at its core a five-step practice that leads people to focus their minds, regulate their breathing, cultivate true qi, and open the channels, thereby uncovering the latent potential within the body and bringing into play a whole series of functions — self-regulation, self-repair, self-healing, self-restoration — so as to prevent and cure illness.

This is a method of self-cultivation and self-nourishment for health and healing, created by Professor Li Shaobo, the distinguished physician and health scholar, who drew upon the theory of “guiding the qi to perfect the true” in the Yellow Emperor’s Inner Canon and the essential teachings of the ancient schools on conducting qi and nourishing life, joined these to his own practice, and refined them through decades of clinical observation and scientific experiment.

Over more than sixty years of clinical application, the Zhenqi Circulation Method has shown notable efficacy against over eighty kinds of chronic, stubborn, and intractable illnesses that had long resisted cure, confirming the reliability and effectiveness of this practice. Grounded in Chinese medical science,

it is prized by the medical profession, the scientific community, and the general public alike for its simplicity, ease of learning, rapid opening of the Governing Vessel, marked efficacy, freedom from side effects, and its suitability for young and old.

blocks.text: The Five Steps and the Three Stages

inline.s: The practice of the Zhenqi Circulation Method is divided into five steps and comprises three great stages of cultivation.
The practice of the Zhenqi Circulation Method is divided into five steps:
The first step: on the exhalation, attend to the region of the heart’s mouth;
The second step: let mind and breath follow together toward the dantian;
The third step: regulate the breath, gather the spirit, and hold to the dantian;
The fourth step: pass the Governing Vessel — neither forget nor help;
The fifth step: the primal spirit gathers power and nurtures the germ of life.
The cultivation of the Zhenqi Circulation Method comprises three great stages:

1. Refining the essence into qi: the first and second steps of the five-step practice regulate the breath so as to impel true qi, causing the true qi within the body to gather in the dantian. This stage was called in antiquity “refining the essence into qi.” It is the first stage, and also the elementary one.

2. Refining the qi into spirit: the third and fourth steps take the true qi amassed in the dantian and thrust it in reverse up through the Governing Vessel straight into the sea of the brain, thereby restoring and strengthening the function of the brain and heightening the protective inhibitory power of the cerebral cortex. This stage is called “refining the qi into spirit.” It is the intermediate stage, and the changes in the body are fairly evident.

3. Refining the spirit into emptiness: with the fifth step and the practice that follows, the skill grows ever more refined and polished. Because the channels are open without obstruction, the various stirring and moving phenomena that arise in practice gradually subside, and the regularity of the circulation of true qi becomes ever more pronounced. Bodily function grows stronger and vitality abounds, while the protective inhibitory power of the cerebral cortex acts all the better; hence the state of stillness becomes the more evident — pure and quiet, the mind like still water. This stage is called “refining the spirit into emptiness” and belongs to the advanced stage of Zhenqi Circulation.

Through these five steps one opens the Small Heavenly Circuit and the Great Heavenly Circuit; and passing through the three stages of refining the essence into qi, refining the qi into spirit, and refining the spirit into emptiness, one gains the benefit of preventing and curing illness, of strengthening the body and lengthening life. The body’s physiological functions undergo the change of returning from the acquired to the innate. Continuing in practice, the principle is to take the practice as the method, stillness as the task, and abiding as the attainment, pressing onward toward the advanced stage of refining the spirit into emptiness, in hope of reaching the ultimate goal of “long life and far-seeing vision, a return to simplicity and the true.”

[The Conception and Governing Vessels] The Conception Vessel (renmai) and the Governing Vessel (dumai). The Conception governs all the yin of the body; the Governing governs all the yang. When the “Conception and Governing Vessels” are opened, qi and blood flow freely. [The Conception Vessel] Beginning at the Chengjiang point below the lip, it runs down the very center of the front of the body to the Huiyin point at the perineum between the legs — this channel is the Conception Vessel. It governs the six yin channels, travels along the center of the abdomen, and has the role of overseeing and managing in general the qi of all the yin channels, regulating their qi and blood; hence it is called the “sea of the yin channels.” [The Governing Vessel] From the Huiyin point the Governing Vessel runs backward and upward along the spine to the Baihui point at the crown of the head, then forward between the eyes to the Yinjiao point in the upper palate of the mouth. It governs the six yang channels,
commanding and impelling the qi of all the yang channels of the body,

so that wherever yang qi is weak one may find a suitable point on the Governing Vessel for treatment. [The Tongue Touching the Upper Palate] In practicing qigong, “setting the tongue against the upper palate” joins the Conception and Governing Vessels, and for this reason it is called “the Magpie Bridge.”

[The Small Heavenly Circuit] First, by refining the essence into qi, one opens the Conception and Governing Vessels. True qi begins at the lower dantian, rises along the Huiyin and Weilü points, passes the Jiaji and Yuzhen, goes through the Baihui, descends the Magpie Bridge, and then follows the Conception Vessel down to the dantian. Circulating in this way along the Conception and Governing Vessels, it is called the “Small Heavenly Circuit.” [The Magpie Bridge] Setting the tongue against the upper palate is called the Magpie Bridge; it draws down the true qi that has come along the Governing Vessel and returns it along the Conception Vessel to the dantian.

[The Great Heavenly Circuit] Building upon the cultivation of the Small Heavenly Circuit, when true qi is set in motion in the dantian a sensation of a warm current arises in that region; one then uses the intention to guide this warm stream through the extraordinary channels and the twelve primary channels throughout the body, circulating over the whole frame in accord with the rule of the rise and fall, the opening and closing, of the qi mechanism. In time the work is accomplished — this is the “Great Heavenly Circuit.” [Far-Seeing Vision] Not to age, and to keep the eyes and ears undimmed — a description of longevity.

One who is beginning the True Method should adopt the correct posture, as a standard for the beginner. The practice of Zhenqi Circulation has four forms — walking, standing, sitting, and lying — of which the sitting posture is primary and the others are subsidiary. To promote the steady progress of true qi circulation efficiently, aside from the sitting posture one may also adopt various postures at any time and in any place.

Sitting: the sitting posture is of two kinds — cross-legged sitting and sitting with the legs hanging. One chooses for oneself according to one’s own custom and circumstances. It is generally felt that cross-legged sitting is rather formal, and that the legs easily become numb and sore; therefore most people adopt the hanging-leg sitting (sitting on a chair or stool), which is conducive to the circulation of true qi and easy to master.

Cross-legged sitting: the “double cross” places the left foot upon the right thigh, then lifts the right foot onto the left thigh, the two hands joined before the lower abdomen. This posture serves only to make the sitting steady and not easily unsettled, yet it is not readily achieved without considerable skill. The “single cross” places the right leg upon the left leg, the hands arranged as before; this is easier to accomplish than the double cross. The “free cross” crosses the two legs one over the other, and is the posture customarily used by most people.

Hanging-leg sitting: the height of the chair or stool should be such that when seated the upper thighs remain level. Sit on the front third of the stool (do not fill the whole seat, nor lean the body against the backrest), so that the hips and thighs rest upon the seat while the lower legs hang outside it. The lower legs hang vertical, forming with the thighs a

angle. The two feet rest flat and parallel on the ground; the distance between the knees is such that two fists (with their eye-holes facing each other) may be set between them. The two palms face downward and rest naturally upon the thighs. The shoulders are relaxed and drooping, the back kept straight without effort, the chin slightly drawn in, and the crown of the head as if suspended. The carriage should be upright, natural, and relaxed. This posture is easy to master, does not easily tire, and is favorable to the circulation of true qi; it is therefore the posture customarily adopted in the present day.

Lying posture: lie on the right side against the bed, with the lower leg extended and the upper leg bent; bend the right arm and set the hand on the pillow just before and below the head, and place the left hand upon the left hip.

Standing posture: the standing posture has many forms, which need not be set out one by one here. Let me only describe a convenient and easy posture, to serve as an aid to the sitting practice. Stand with the feet together and the two hands placed over the dantian (the left palm over the dantian, the right palm upon the back of the left hand). Relax the shoulders, let the elbows droop, soften the chest and straighten the back, empty the heart and fill the abdomen, and let the eyes be as if behind lowered curtains.

Walking posture: when walking or strolling, gaze three to five steps ahead, keep the mind upon the tip of the nose, and let the spirit not be distracted abroad; take one breath over four steps and one exhalation over four steps. If one can practice this method over a long period, it greatly aids in walking long distances, so that one may go on without weariness.

blocks.text: The Requirements for the Five Senses

inline.s: Mouth: let the lips close naturally and the upper and lower teeth meet; curl the tongue upward to about ninety degrees, and with the tip gently press the upper palate (as shown in the figure below). When the saliva increases, put the tongue down and slowly swallow, then continue to press the tongue against the upper palate.

Eyes: half-close them and look within; whichever step one is practicing, direct the inner gaze upon that corresponding region. For instance, in the first step, when attending to the heart’s-mouth region, look within upon the heart’s-mouth region.

Ears: let both ears heed the breath, seeing that it makes no coarse sound yet without causing any holding of it; keep the breathing calm and natural — this is an excellent method for gathering the mind.

Since the breath is the motive power that impels the circulation of true qi, the cultivation of the True Method lays great stress upon breathing. Throughout the practice of the True Method one breathes in and out through the nose;

in the whole of the five-step practice one attends only to the exhalation and pays no heed to the inhalation, letting it take its natural course, so that no fault arises. This very point — “attend only to the exhalation, pay no heed to the inhalation” — is of great importance, lest such undesirable effects as holding the breath should appear.

Once the true qi in the dantian is replenished, it naturally opens through the Governing Vessel. At that time one feels that with each exhalation true qi enters the dantian, and with each inhalation it travels along the Governing Vessel into the brain. This is the natural activity of true qi and need not be sought after. The breath then becomes fine and continuous, as if present and yet as if absent, and grows ever more natural; at this point one has no further need to pay attention to the breath.

As to the manner of breathing, this essay introduces the reverse abdominal breathing; but if one finds the reverse abdominal breathing difficult, one may use the thoracic breathing that most people employ in everyday life.

[Thoracic breathing] Chiefly involving the movement of the ribs and sternum, the chest cavity expands on inhalation and contracts on exhalation, while the abdomen remains flat throughout. For the harms of thoracic breathing, see the article
Abdominal Breathing
and the accompanying discussion on “the harms of thoracic breathing.”
The reverse abdominal breathing is described below:

Reverse abdominal breathing, also called dantian breathing. On inhalation, draw the abdomen in and tighten the perineum; on exhalation, swell the abdomen and relax the perineum. When one first uses the reverse abdominal breathing for the five-step practice of Zhenqi Circulation, one should not seek fineness, evenness, depth, and length; it is enough that the abdomen begins to move, for at this point the Conception Vessel is not yet open. As the skill deepens, the breath naturally grows ever deeper and longer, and the number of breaths per minute grows fewer and fewer, gradually attaining fineness, evenness, depth, and length.

In the early practice, the swelling and contracting of the lower abdomen may be fairly pronounced; once one is skilled, one may lessen the amplitude, gradually arriving at the state of “as if it has and yet has not, as if it lacks and yet lacks not.” At that time the whole body is relaxed and free-flowing.

[The Huiyin Point] The Huiyin point is an important acupoint on the Conception Vessel of the human body. It lies in the hollow midway between the anus and the genitals. The Huiyin point forms a straight line with the Baihui point at the crown of the head, and is the passageway of the body’s essence, qi, and spirit. Baihui is yang and receives the qi of heaven; Huiyin is yin and gathers the qi of earth. The two depend on each other, correspond and answer each other, and together govern the normal circulation of true qi along the Conception and Governing Vessels, maintaining within the body the balance of yin and yang, of qi and blood. It is a vital part of the body’s life activity. Li Shizhen, in his Study of the Eight Extraordinary Channels, sets forth that the Huiyin point is where the Conception, Governing, and Penetrating Vessels meet, an important point upon the eight extraordinary channels; that it is the source whence vitality springs, maintaining the balance of qi and blood, of yin and yang, and is therefore also a key point for longevity. “Huiyin” is the name used in Chinese medicine; the Daoists call it the “yin heel,” and in the Yogic schools it is called the “root chakra.” Every school and lineage praises greatly the cultivation of this region.

The method of reverse abdominal breathing changes the volume of the abdominal cavity while breathing, yet its focus is not upon the air drawn in and out, but upon true qi (the inner qi). Hence, although in name the reverse abdominal breathing is a way of breathing air, in substance it is the “breathing” of the inner qi — its rising and falling, its swelling and surging. Reverse abdominal breathing is highly beneficial to body and mind; there are those who, practicing it alone, have cured many chronic illnesses. To dispel disease and prolong life, one should do the reverse abdominal breathing as often as possible in daily life.

If one is still unaccustomed to the reverse abdominal breathing, one should set aside time to practice this manner of breathing by itself, exercising for a few minutes whenever the chance arises; the more times each day one practices, the better. Gradually it becomes easy and natural, until at last it has taken root as habit.

In the early stage of learning, one may silently recite the word “draw in” on the inhalation and the word “swell” on the exhalation, thus helping to bring about the action of drawing the abdomen in on the inhale and swelling it on the exhale.

The basic point of focus of the Zhenqi Circulation Method is the dantian, and since it does not draw qi outward from the dantian, it does not perform a concluding exercise of returning qi to the dantian. Before each session of practice ends, first relax the mind, rub the palms of the hands together until warm, then stroke the face in a washing motion several times, and comb the hair with the ten fingers for a moment; once the spirit has returned to its ordinary state, rise slowly and move about as one pleases.

The rule of true qi circulation is this: in the qigong state of quiet and empty stillness, true qi is produced and gathered in the dantian, and runs along the Conception and Governing Vessels and the twelve primary channels, arising and transforming of itself, regulating the body, dispelling disease, and prolonging life. Therefore the key to cultivating the True Method is to enter into and abide in the qigong state of quiet and empty stillness.
The Inner Canon says:
“In calm detachment and empty nothingness, true qi follows it; when the spirit is guarded within, whence can illness come?”

Therefore the whole aim of the Zhenqi Circulation Method from beginning to end is to overcome stray thoughts and enter stillness. Abundant practice has shown that among practitioners, the better one’s stillness, the faster one’s power grows. So whatever step one is practicing, one must lay effort upon entering stillness.

[Calm detachment and empty nothingness] This is the state of “no thought arising, self and things both forgotten, dim and obscure.” “Calm detachment” (tiandan) means tranquil and at ease; “empty” (xu) means self and things both forgotten; “nothing” (wu) means having no deluded thoughts (no thought arising). [True qi follows it] When one is in the state of “no thought arising, self and things both forgotten, dim and obscure,” true qi naturally circulates along the channels,
regulating the body, dispelling disease, and prolonging life,

and so on. [The spirit guarded within] A person’s spirit and qi are originally one; when the spirit rushes abroad, the qi wanders abroad as well, and with the spirit and qi leaking outward, the body is worn away. Therefore one should keep the spirit and qi held within, so as to preserve abundant true qi, make the body’s power to resist disease strong, and then illness has no way to arise — thus attaining health and long life.
The signs of the completion of each step are as follows:
First step (on the exhalation, attend to the heart’s-mouth region): the sensation of qi in the heart’s-mouth region naturally moves toward the lower dantian.
Second step (let mind and breath follow together toward the dantian): a clear sensation of qi appears in the lower dantian.

Third step (regulate the breath, gather the spirit, and hold to the dantian): there arise the phenomena of the perineum jumping and the qi stirring at the sacrum (indicating that true qi has entered the Governing Vessel).
Fourth step (pass the Governing Vessel — neither forget nor help): the Governing Vessel is passed.

At the beginning of each session, first half-close the eyes as behind lowered curtains, letting through a sliver of light, gently gaze at the tip of the nose, draw the spirit inward and still the mind, and then practice according to the method.

blocks.text: Step One: On the Exhalation, Attend to the Heart’s-Mouth Region

inline.s: The heart’s-mouth region, that is, the area over the pit of the heart, is a region centered upon the Juque point. It is a region, not a single point.

Method: when the practice is ready, half-close both eyes, first gaze at the tip of the nose for a moment, then, with the eyes closed, look within upon the heart’s-mouth region, and let the ears listen to the breath without letting it make a sound. With each exhalation, let the intention, following the breath, descend from the throat to the heart’s-mouth region; as for the inhalation, let it take its own course and pay it no heed. Because of the pressure difference between the atmospheric pressure outside the body and the intra-pulmonary pressure within, whatever stale air is breathed out, so much fresh air is drawn in; this is a natural method of breath regulation in accord with physiology, and it is the particular method of breath regulation of the Zhenqi Circulation Method. The breathing is natural breathing; one should not deliberately lengthen the exhalation or the inhalation, otherwise such discomforts as holding the breath will arise. If stray thoughts come during practice, subdue them by counting the breaths: simply count the exhalations, from
then turn back and again from
repeating in this way; once the stray thoughts are calmed, there is no need to count the breaths.

[Natural breathing] This simply means not deliberately controlling the depth, rhythm, and so on of the breath, but letting it take its natural course. As the skill deepens and true qi grows abundant, the breath becomes as if present and yet as if absent, fine and long, and its frequency naturally decreases. This natural process draws in more oxygen, so that one not only feels no holding of the breath, but feels all the more comfortable. One should understand that the number of breaths cannot be artificially increased or decreased; it must be natural. To deliberately pursue deep breathing or slow breathing runs counter to physiology.

Time: to complete the practice of the first step on schedule, some arrangement of time is needed. If circumstances permit, practicing at a fixed time each day to form the habit is all the more helpful for steadying the mind. Should there be no fixed time, it is of no account; one has only to seize spare moments and practice diligently. One is asked to practice three times a day — morning, midday, and evening — for twenty minutes each time. If carried out earnestly, in about a week the stage of the first step can be completed.

Response: after three to five days of practice one feels a heaviness in the heart’s-mouth region; further on, with each exhalation one senses a warm current flowing into the heart’s-mouth region — this is the sign of true qi concentrating. With the true qi thus gathered, the foundation for the second step is laid.

Effects: in the first few days, owing to unfamiliarity and a posture not yet precise, some may feel giddiness, soreness in the back and loins, breathing that is not natural, or the tip of the tongue unable to press the upper palate — all these are natural phenomena. Have no misgivings; so long as one perseveres in practice in accordance with the instructions, in time all will be well.
When the sensation of qi in the heart’s-mouth region naturally moves toward the lower dantian, it marks the completion of the first step.

blocks.text: Step Two: Let Mind and Breath Follow Together Toward the Dantian

inline.s: The dantian referred to here is the lower dantian. The lower dantian is the Guanyuan point of the Conception Vessel, located three inches (four fingers’ width) below the navel, that is, at the very center of the lower abdomen — the dwelling place where essence is stored. The lower dantian is the principal region where true qi is worked upon, gathered, and stored.

Let mind and breath follow together toward the dantian” means: the mind (yi) follows the exhalation (xi) downward and guides the true qi (manifest as a warm sensation in the heart’s-mouth region) into the dantian. The purpose of this step is to send the true qi gathered in the heart’s-mouth region down along the Conception Vessel to the dantian, in order to open the Conception Vessel.

The circulation of true qi requires the breath to impel it and the mind to guide it. Hence in the Zhenqi Circulation Method the breath and the mind are of great importance. The movement of true qi in the channel passages
is driven by the breath: on exhalation, true qi moves downward and outward; on inhalation, true qi moves upward and inward.

Method: when the first step has been practiced to the point that each exhalation brings a felt warmth in the heart’s-mouth region, one may then let mind and breath follow together; with each exhalation, use the mind to guide the warm current of the heart’s-mouth region to extend gradually downward, moving step by step toward the dantian. But one must remain relaxed and natural, not use the mind too forcefully nor act with haste, for too great an exertion will produce excessive heat and a sense of discomfort.
Time: practicing in accordance with the method three times a day, for twenty-five or thirty minutes each time, in about ten days the qi can settle into the dantian.

Effects: since true qi has passed through the stomach region, the function of the spleen and stomach has already improved. After true qi settles into the dantian, the surrounding organs — the large and small intestines, the bladder, the kidneys, and so on — gradually undergo physiological changes; generally one feels an increase in appetite, and the abnormalities of urination and defecation improve to varying degrees.
When a clear sensation of qi appears in the lower dantian, it marks the completion of the second step.

At this point the qi settles into the dantian; the dantian, receiving the impact of true qi, gives rise to a sensation, and the site of the dantian is made evident. Yet in an instant the impact, or the swelling-warm sensation, of the dantian soon vanishes again. When the dantian has qi it opens; when it has no qi it closes. The true qi descending from the middle dantian (the heart’s-mouth region) along the Conception Vessel enters the lower dantian, yet is not enough to swell and fill it, so the pressure in the dantian disappears or becomes very slight, and the sensation of qi at once fades. But this shows that true qi has sunk to the lower dantian and the Conception Vessel is open, and so one may proceed to the practice of the third step.

blocks.text: Step Three: Regulate the Breath, Gather the Spirit, and Hold to the Dantian

inline.s: Throughout the five-step practice of Zhenqi Circulation, the focus is always upon abiding mentally with the dantian. Even after the Conception and Governing Vessels are opened, for a considerable period the practice still centers upon abiding mentally with the dantian. Hence “regulate the breath, gather the spirit, and hold to the dantian” is forever the heart of the method.

Regulate the breath” means grasping well the force with which the qi moves toward the dantian. “Gather the spirit and hold to the dantian” means no longer attending to the exhalation, but concentrating the mind to abide with the dantian, not letting the spirit wander abroad.
[Abiding mentally with the dantian] Place the attention upon the region of the dantian and watch over it here.

Method: at the start of the third step, one uses the method of the previous step (“let mind and breath follow together toward the dantian”) to send true qi into the dantian. At this point one employs a strong intention and a heavy, urgent exhalation (the stirring of the martial fire). When the sensation of warmth from true qi in the lower dantian is clear and steady, one then adjusts the force of “let mind and breath follow together toward the dantian,” slowing the exhalation and relaxing the intention of guiding the qi toward the dantian (the gentle warming of the civil fire), so as to keep the dantian warm without letting it burn, lest the dantian overheat and injure the fluids of yin, committing the fault of “the raging fire devouring the qi.” Then one goes on to cease attending to the exhalation and abide mentally with the dantian (“gather the spirit and hold to the dantian”), gradually reaching the state of guarding as if not guarding, fine and continuous as if present (it is enough that the dantian remain warm). Because at this point the Conception Vessel is already open and the qi has settled into the dantian, simply abiding mentally with the dantian suffices to fill it. The degree of fire is best when the dantian is warm without burning hot. If one feels that the dantian lacks qi, one uses “let mind and breath follow together toward the dantian” to replenish true qi into the dantian, making it full and complete.

In “abiding mentally with the dantian” one must also grasp well the intensity of the abiding, that is, the intensity of the attention while abiding. If the intensity is too slight, stray thoughts are hard to dispel and the dantian hard to hold; if the intensity is somewhat too great, then although stray thoughts may be reduced, it is apt to bring on such discomforts as headache, swelling in the head, and nervous tension. Therefore in the early practice the intensity should be somewhat greater than “as if present and yet as if absent,” and the mind should be relaxed, taking as the measure the absence of swelling and pain in the head; this helps to dispel stray thoughts and to aid entering stillness. As the skill deepens, one may gradually lessen the intensity of the abiding.

Time: three times a day, or a few more, each session over half an hour. This stage is the period of building the strength of the dantian and requires a fairly long time; in about a month one can feel the lower abdomen full and powerful.

Effects: because the Conception Vessel is open, the heart and kidney interact, and the middle qi is vigorous, the mind and spirit are tranquil and sleep is still. Those who suffer from heart fire flaming upward, from insomnia and excessive dreaming, and from irregularities of the heart all improve. Through the continuous addition of warmth to the stomach and intestines by practice, the digestive and absorptive capacity of the spleen and stomach increases; body weight increases, the spirit is full, the innate qi is abundant, and kidney function is strengthened. Those afflicted with impotence have marked improvement, and irregular menstruation in women improves to varying degrees. The kidney water being abundant, the liver receives its nourishment. Hence, at this stage those with chronic hepatitis and early cirrhosis show distinct improvement; if one persists in practice, they naturally heal.

[The interaction of heart and kidney] The heart belongs to fire and stores the spirit; the kidney belongs to water and stores the essence. These two organs interact with and restrain each other so as to maintain normal physiological activity. The true yang within the kidney, rising upward, can warm and nourish the heart fire; the heart fire can restrain the flooding of the kidney water and assist the true yang; and the kidney water can restrain the heart fire so that it does not become excessive, thereby nourishing the heart yin. This relationship is also called “water and fire aiding each other.” If the balance of yin and yang in either the heart or the kidney is upset, the “water and fire in mutual harmony” relationship between heart and kidney is broken and corresponding illnesses appear; this is called “the heart and kidney not interacting” or “water and fire not in harmony.”
When the phenomena of the perineum jumping and the qi stirring at the sacrum appear, this indicates that true qi has entered the Governing Vessel, and marks the completion of the third step.

blocks.text: Step Four: Pass the Governing Vessel — Neither Forget Nor Help

inline.s: Method: continuing from the previous step (“regulate the breath, gather the spirit, and hold to the dantian”), when the true qi in the dantian has been replenished to a certain degree, it will ascend along the spine. At this point the intention should follow the sensation of qi: when the qi moves, follow its movement; when the qi stops, follow its stopping (do not forget), and do not use the intention to guide it upward (do not help). For the swiftness of the ascent depends entirely upon the degree to which the true qi in the dantian is replenished: the more fully replenished the dantian’s true qi, the greater the ascending force and the faster the speed. Otherwise the ascent ceases midway, or even retreats; once the true qi in the dantian is replenished, it will naturally continue upward. If one impetuously seeks to pass the pass and guides upward, one becomes detached from the strength of the dantian — pulling up the sprouts to help them grow — which is very harmful. When the true qi ascends to the “Yuzhen Pass” behind the head and, repeatedly striving upward, finds it hard to pass through, one may use the method of looking within upon the crown of the head, and as a rule the Yuzhen Pass is then crossed.

The key to this step is: neither forget nor help, and follow what is natural. There is no need to trouble oneself about passing the Governing Vessel; so long as the true qi in the dantian is full and strong, it will pass through of itself. If the true qi lingers at some place, it shows that the true qi in the dantian is not yet sufficient, that it has not yet reached the strength needed to pass the Governing Vessel,
in which case one should again practice the third step (“regulate the breath, gather the spirit, and hold to the dantian”)

to build up the strength of the dantian so as to pass the Governing Vessel. If one forcibly guides upward, it is not only fruitless but harmful. One who studies on his own, meeting such a circumstance, should by no means seek others to “help,” for that will be of no avail. Only by one’s own effort —
practicing the third step (“regulate the breath, gather the spirit, and hold to the dantian”)
— is there any remedy.

Time: the number of daily sessions may be increased as appropriate, and each session extended to forty minutes or about an hour. Each person’s circumstances differ, so the time and strength of passing the Governing Vessel cannot be the same. Some pass it in an instant, with great force and a strong vibration; others take somewhat longer and with less force. Most people pass the Governing Vessel in about ten days.

Effects: once the Governing Vessel is open, with one exhalation true qi goes down along the Conception Vessel into the dantian, and with one inhalation true qi ascends along the Governing Vessel to the Baihui. Each inhalation and exhalation forms a Conception–Governing circulation, which the world of health-preserving practitioners calls the “Small Heavenly Circuit.” Only in this condition can one actually sense the reality of “breathing in the essence of qi and keeping the spirit in solitary guard.” True qi ceaselessly replenishes the brain marrow (returning the essence to nourish the brain), and the innate power of the cerebral cortex is strengthened. All the neurotic symptoms arising from the depletion of kidney essence and disturbance of the endocrine system — giddiness and tinnitus, insomnia and forgetfulness, sore loins and weak legs, irregular menstruation, a dazed spirit, easy joy and easy anger, a fluttering heart and short breath, a decline of desire — may all be improved. With long persistence one may recover. Because the channels are open through practice, some stubborn ailments that had persisted for years may suddenly be cured, with marked effect. In general one shows abundant energy and a light, agile body.

The experience of passing the Governing Vessel differs from person to person: at the Yuzhen some hear a “whoosh,” as if a cannon had gone off; others feel a creeping like ants, or a line slowly passing through. This is only a difference in the strength of the force. As long as one feels the current of qi pass the Yuzhen Pass, one has passed the Governing Vessel. After passing, the current of qi travels along the Conception and Governing Vessels, and the sensation in the dantian becomes less distinct.
Passing the Governing Vessel marks the completion of the fourth step.

The Conception Vessel is the sea of all the yin channels, the Governing Vessel the meeting place of all the yang channels; when the Conception and Governing Vessels are unobstructed, the twelve primary channels can one by one become unobstructed as well, and then illness has nowhere to lodge, and health and long life are assured. Zhuangzi says:
“Follow the central channel as your path: thus you may preserve your body, thus you may keep whole your life, thus you may nourish your kin, thus you may fulfill your years.”
(“Nourishing the Lord of Life”)

blocks.text: Step Five: The Primal Spirit Gathers Power and Nurtures the Germ of Life

inline.s: The so-called primal spirit is the innate power by which the brain regulates and governs, and it stands opposed to the consciousness-spirit. The consciousness-spirit is the deliberate, thinking state of mind. Primal spirit and consciousness-spirit stand in the relation of substance and function: the primal spirit is the substance, the consciousness-spirit the function. When there is no thought, it is the primal spirit; if a thought stirs even slightly, the primal spirit is transformed into the consciousness-spirit. In the fourth step the Governing Vessel has already been opened, kidney qi ceaselessly irrigates the brain marrow, and the power of the primal spirit is ceaselessly replenished. The heart governs the spirit-mind; only when heart qi shines upward upon the brain can that comprehensive power of regulation and governance come into play.

The meaning of “the primal spirit gathers power and nurtures the germ of life” is this: the mental and conscious state of deep stillness, of “calm detachment and empty nothingness,” is precisely the primal spirit, and it can cause the material and dynamic constituents of life — essence, qi, and spirit — to be gathered and fused together, thereby nurturing a vigorous vitality. This step of practice (“the primal spirit gathers power and nurtures the germ of life”) is carried out in a state of deep stillness.

[Entering stillness] This refers to a state in qigong practice that arises upon a foundation of mental quiet and concentrated intention — a state clear and wakeful, with the intention held single, relaxed and at ease. Entering stillness differs both from ordinary wakefulness and from falling asleep. It is not the cessation of all thought, nor is it dullness or confusion; rather, one thought replaces ten thousand thoughts, and the intention of practice is still retained. For the practitioner: if in the course of practice even the intention of practice is lost, it is like a ship that has lost its rudder, so that in a dazed and drifting condition deviations may arise — this is something to be watched for.
Method: once the Conception–Governing circulation has been formed, one generally still abides mentally with the lower dantian,
and at this point there is no further need to attend to the breath

After the Governing Vessel is passed, the various channels open one after another; if there is an active force at the Baihui point on the crown of the head, one may abide mentally with the Baihui as well. This is to grasp the practice flexibly, and it is what is called “when there is desire, observe the opening; when there is no desire, observe the wonder.” As the skill advances, one will naturally strengthen body and health and unfold wisdom, and ever finer and more wondrous states will appear.

[The upper dantian] The upper dantian is the place where the hundred channels converge; to abide constantly with this opening can unfold wisdom, preserve life, and harmonize and penetrate the primordial whole. When the true qi of the upper dantian is lively and the innate power of the brain functions well, the regulation and management of the whole body is the better. [When there is desire, observe the opening; when there is no desire, observe the wonder] This means: in practice, if stray thoughts arise, then abide mentally with the lower dantian, using one thought to replace ten thousand thoughts; and once one has entered stillness and the upper dantian begins to respond, one may quietly abide with the upper dantian and taste that mysterious state.

Time: three times a day, or a little more, each session an hour or longer. On the whole, the longer the time the better. Only after about a month do the various stirring phenomena within the body gradually disappear, leaving only the phenomenon of the power of the lower and upper dantian growing more concentrated and vigorous.

Effects: judging by what appears in the body — especially the magnetic force of mutual attraction between the dantian and the Baihui point on the crown of the head — the innate power of the cerebral cortex is strengthened, and the endocrine system is harmonious and vigorous. This force has form and color; the deeper the skill, the more evident and lively its manifestations, the better the regulation of the physiological functions of the whole body, and the more abundant the true qi becomes, ceaselessly supplementing and strengthening the body’s metabolic functions, so that the latent powers of the organism may come fully into play. Because vitality is vigorous, resistance to illness and immune power are strengthened; ordinary pathogenic factors may be reduced or even avoided, and chronic ailments of long standing may be improved or cured. With persistent practice one may attain the effects of physical and mental health and of lengthened life.

The five steps above are a basic outline of the practice of the quiet cultivation of the True Method. In actual practice, since each person’s constitution differs and the particular circumstances differ as well, the effects and manifestations differ from person to person, though in the main they are much the same. In view of this, one should in practice both follow what is natural and apply the method flexibly, without rigidly clinging to it, and also hold to certain requirements, advancing with patience and persevering to the end, never letting things drift — this is truly the key to success.

In practicing the True Method one must establish unshakable confidence and persevere to the end, neither seeking quick results nor retreating when difficulties arise. Throughout the period of practice, follow what is natural, and do not cling to deluded thoughts or force what cannot be forced. Otherwise, haste defeats its own purpose: the more one chases after results and the more impatient one becomes, the less progress one makes; whereas the more harmonious and natural one’s state of mind, the livelier the true qi’s arising, and the more evident one’s progress. For clinging to deluded thoughts becomes a stray thought that disturbs the movement of true qi. “In calm detachment and empty nothingness, true qi follows it” — this is exactly what is meant.

In the course of practice, because many physiological changes occur in the body and various stirring phenomena appear, one should take them calmly, neither falling into a panic nor clinging to them in pursuit; after a short while they will pass of themselves.

. In first learning the True Method, since the mind must be concentrated, it is better to have a comparatively quiet environment. But do not overstress this point. During practice, avoid interference from others. If some unexpected disturbance occurs in the midst of practice (a sudden noise, someone shouting urgently, someone bursting into the practice room, and the like), then do not be alarmed: slowly relax the intention. Conclude the practice for the time being, then rise slowly and attend to the matter, and when calm has been restored, make up the practice. In regulating the breath, breathe in and out through the nose, attend to the exhalation, and let the inhalation take its own course; do not breathe through the mouth.

. Take care not to force the practice when in the grip of such emotional surges as extreme hunger, extreme fullness, great anger, or great shock. When there is wind, rain, or thunder, for the time being do not sit in practice, lest the spirit receive a violent shock and discomfort arise.

. Abiding mentally with the dantian is a principle that the True Method maintains throughout. When the true qi in the dantian is replenished to a certain degree, it will naturally run along the channels. The force of this movement is determined by the strength of the dantian. Do not use the intention to guide it; let it take its own course — when it should move, let it move; when it should stop, let it stop. Subjective guiding will produce deviations.

. One who uses this method, before passing the pass, must conserve his vital power and restrain sexual activity, lest the progress of practice be affected. If a woman is menstruating, she should not abide mentally with the lower dantian; she may abide with the middle dantian (the heart’s-mouth region). In the early stage of pregnancy (
months) one cannot practice; in the middle and later stages one may.

In the course of cultivating the five-step practice, the dynamic phenomena within the body are of many kinds; the ancients summed them up as eight and called them the “eight sensations.” At one moment one feels the body to be very “large,” at another very “small”; sometimes one feels the body to be very “light,” sometimes the body appears “heavy” as a great boulder; sometimes one feels the body to be very “cool,” while the sensation of “heat” appears the fastest and most often of all; and there are also the sensations of “itching” and “numbness.” Beyond these “eight sensations,” the dynamics in actual practice are more numerous still — spontaneous movement, perceptions of light, and also residual and unusual phenomena.

The phenomena described above are all manifestations of true qi moving within the body in different forms, and all are positive and beneficial. Some people, meeting with such phenomena, send for a doctor; the doctor does not understand, and recklessly administers medicines — this is harmful. Some do not understand the principle and make of it a mental burden. Some are curious and chase after these phenomena, and the more attention they pay the more intense they become, until they can no longer be controlled. All these cases come of the principle not having been clearly explained. Once one understands the laws of the movement of true qi, one can avoid mistaken thoughts and behavior. When such stirring phenomena occur, there is no need to pursue them out of curiosity, and still less to fall into a panic; one has only to sit quietly in practice, abiding mentally with the dantian, and after a time they subside.

blocks.text: The Relation of Movement and Stillness

inline.s: Movement and stillness are the two aspects, at once opposed and united, of the motion of things in the universe. The True Method makes effective use of the relation between stillness and movement to promote the circulation of true qi and to enable the organism to bring its vital powers better into play, so as to dispel illness and lengthen life.

Where there is movement there must be stillness, and where there is stillness there must be movement. When stillness reaches its extreme, movement arises; when movement reaches its extreme, stillness returns. Stillness is the foundation of movement, and movement is the manifestation of the power of stillness. Movement is absolute, stillness is relative. In the physiological activity of the human body, too, this law cannot be escaped. The bodily form belongs to yin and is of the nature of stillness; true qi belongs to yang and is of the nature of movement. When qi leaves the form, it has nothing to depend upon; when the form is without qi, it becomes a mere inert lump. Only when yin and yang are rooted in each other, when stillness and movement nurture each other, and when form and qi coexist, is there a lively vitality throughout.

The stillness spoken of in the five-step practice of True Qi Circulation means simply calming the body, concentrating the whole spirit upon regulating the breath, impelling the circulation of true qi, opening through the Conception and Governing Vessels, and penetrating the channels. In this process the stirring phenomena within the body are of many kinds, and the functions of every part of the body are in a state of active, vigorous, and abundant life. How could this be any mere stillness and concentration? It is nothing but a circulation of true qi that is exceedingly vigorous, exceedingly natural, and exceedingly regular — this is what is called “when stillness reaches its extreme, movement arises.” The so-called stillness can only be called a temporary and relative stillness with respect to reactions to the outer world or to the activity of thought.

The movement of a living body is absolute, its stillness relative. One who practices quiet cultivation, though there be no movement of posture, still passes from the deliberate to the non-deliberate. In the course of practice, as true qi is cultivated and the channels are penetrated, there is exceedingly intense activity at the three dantians in front and the three gates behind. Especially when storming the three gates behind, the force of the true qi’s activity does not follow a person’s will; rather, one is controlled by a powerful surging force. And this force is formed by “when stillness reaches its extreme, movement arises” and “when movement reaches its extreme, stillness returns.” People are well acquainted with stillness giving rise to movement and welcome it, knowing that one must rely on this motive force to storm the gates; but before the phenomenon of movement returning to stillness they are utterly in the dark, and doubt arises and they do not know what to do. In truth, when things have moved to a certain degree, they must of necessity grow still, to rest and recover and so be the better able to move again. This is an everyday natural phenomenon. After true qi has been active for a time, it must settle and grow still, to recover and build up a greater force. Therefore, if in the course of practice one suddenly finds the sensations in the dantian vanish or the true qi moving in fits and starts, all this is normal and no doubt should be entertained. One has only to continue quietly cultivating the strength of the dantian, and the true qi will of itself grow lively again.

In sum, the successive levels of the True Qi Circulation Method — refining the essence into qi, refining the qi into spirit, and refining the spirit into emptiness — are all accomplished by bringing into play the natural laws of “when stillness reaches its extreme, movement arises,” “when movement reaches its extreme, stillness returns,” and “stillness and movement nurture each other.”
Clinical verification has shown marked therapeutic effects upon over

kinds of functional and organic disorders: hypertension, heart disease, diabetes, pulmonary tuberculosis, emphysema, diseases of the liver and gallbladder, early cirrhosis, gastrointestinal disease, diseases of the urogenital and reproductive systems, chronic nephritis, rheumatoid arthritis, cervical spondylosis, neurotic symptoms, endocrine disorders, stubborn skin diseases, and so on. More encouraging still, it can also stimulate the body’s interferon and raise immune function, and it has a very good effect both upon the treatment of early-stage cancer patients and upon their recovery after surgery. Therefore the five-step practice of the study of True Qi Circulation is markedly effective in curing various chronic and stubborn illnesses and intractable complaints, and has efficacy against acute diseases as well; moreover, it treats both root and branch, and has no side effects whatever.
